'''Manute Bol''' ({{IPAc-en|m|ə|ˈ|n|uː|t|_|ˈ|b|oʊ|l}}; d. June 19, 2010) was a Sudanese-born American [[basketball]] player and political [[activist]]. Listed at {{height|ft=7|in=7}} tall, Bol was one of the two tallest players in the history of the [[National Basketball Association]].

After playing college basketball at the [[University of Bridgeport]], Bol was chosen by the [[Washington Bullets]] in the 1985 NBA Draft. Bol played for the Bullets and three other teams over the course of his NBA career, which lasted from 1985 to 1995. A [[center (basketball)|center]], Bol was considered among the best shot-blockers in the history of the sport, although other aspects of his game were considered below average. 

Over the course of his career, Bol totaled more blocked shots than points scored; he is the only NBA player ever to do so. As of 2010, he ranks second in NBA history in [[block (basketball)|blocked shots]] per game and 15th in [[List of National Basketball Association career blocks leaders|total blocked shots]].

Bol was notable for his efforts to promote human rights in his native Sudan and aid for Sudanese refugees. 

==Early life==
Manute Bol was born to Madute and Okwok Bol in Turalei or Gogrial, Sudan and raised near Gogrial. Bol's father, a [[Dinka people|Dinka]] tribal elder, gave him the name Manute; the name means "special blessing".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-2002-03-31-0203310024-story.html|title=FOR MANUTE BOL, A HARROWING COMEBACK|first=LYNNE TUOHY; Courant Staff|last=Writer|date=|website=courant.com|accessdate=7 February 2019}}</ref>

Bol came from a family of extraordinarily tall men and women, stating: "My mother was {{height|ft=6|in=10}}, my father {{height|ft=6|in=8}}, and my sister is {{height|ft=6|in=8}}", he said. "And my great-grandfather was even taller—{{height|ft=7|in=10}}." His ethnic group, the Dinka, and the [[Nilotic peoples|Nilotic people]]<ref>{{cite journal |last = Roberts |first = D. F. |author2=D. R. Bainbridge |title = Nilotic physique |journal = Am. J. Phys. Anthropol. |volume = 21 |issue = 3 |pages = 341–70 |date = Sep 1963 |doi = 10.1002/ajpa.1330210309 }}</ref> of which they are a part, are among the taller populations of the world. Bol's hometown, Turalei, is the origin of other exceptionally tall individuals, including {{height|ft=7|in=4}} basketball player Ring Ayuel. Ayuel is a refugee from the [[Second Sudanese Civil War|civil war]] which broke out soon after Bol emigrated to the U.S. and which eventually led to the destruction of most of Turalei.<ref>{{cite web|last=Steward |first=Carl |title=His spirit, giant: Sudanese player embraced at Ohlone College |publisher=Inside Bay Area (via Ohlone College) |date=12 Jan 2011 |url=http://www.ohlone.edu/org/athletics/mensbasketball/teamnews20102011/20110112sudaneseplayer.html |accessdate=2013-01-02 |deadurl=yes |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131018030948/http://www.ohlone.edu/org/athletics/mensbasketball/teamnews20102011/20110112sudaneseplayer.html |archivedate=2013-10-18 |df= }}</ref>

Bol started playing [[Association football|soccer]] in 1972, but abandoned the game because he was too tall.<ref>{{cite news |title = Sudan's NBA giant |newspaper = BBC News |date = 29 Oct 2001 |url = http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/1626514.stm }}</ref> 

"I was born in a village, where you cannot measure yourself," Bol reflected. "I learned I was 7 foot 7 in 1979, when I was grown. I was about 18 or 19."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-2002-03-31-0203310024-story.html|title=FOR MANUTE BOL, A HARROWING COMEBACK|first=LYNNE TUOHY; Courant Staff|last=Writer|website=courant.com}}</ref>

During his later teens, he started playing basketball, playing in Sudan for several years with teams in [[Wau, Sudan|Wau]] and [[Khartoum]], where he experienced prejudice from the northern Sudanese majority.<ref>{{cite book |last = |first = |title = Contemporary Black Biography |chapter = Manute Bol |publisher = Thomson Gale |edition = |location = Detroit |pages = |url = |isbn = }}</ref> 

While still living in Sudan, Bol apparently held an $80-a-month (1983 US$) job in the Sudanese military and played on the Sudanese National basketball team from 1982-1983.<ref name="USAToday">{{cite news|title=Scouts: Bol has slim chance at success|date=April 12, 1985|first=Kathy|last=Blumenstock|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|page=}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=https://www.thedraftreview.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=2159:manute-bol&catid=89&Itemid=342|title=Manute Bol|first1=Fine Line Websites & IT|last1=Consulting|first2=The Draft|last2=Review|website=The Draft Review}}</ref>

==Cleveland / 1983 NBA draft voided==
===Cleveland State===
Coach [[Don Feeley]], formerly the coach at [[Fairleigh Dickinson University]] in [[New Jersey]], traveled to Sudan to coach and held clinics for the Sudanese national team in 1982. Feeley eventually convinced Bol to go to the United States and play basketball.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.answers.com/topic/manute-bol|title=Answers - The Most Trusted Place for Answering Life's Questions|website=Answers.com|accessdate=27 August 2017}}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{cite web|url=https://plus2clothing.com/happened-manute-bol/|title=What Happened to Manute Bol|first=Steve|last=Rogers|date=7 April 2016|website=Plus 2 Clothing}}</ref>

With Feeley's input, Bol first landed in [[Cleveland]] and [[Cleveland State University]] under Coach [[Kevin Mackey]]. Bol had no formal record of his birth date and could not provide one, according to Coach Mackey. As Bol did not know his date of birth, Mackey listed it as October 16, 1962 on Cleveland State documents; however, Mackey believed Bol was actually much older.<ref name="NYDN birthday"/><ref name="Y birthday"/><ref name="cbssports.com"/> 

Bol did not speak or write English at the time of his arrival in Cleveland. He improved his English skills after months of classes at [[ELS Language Centers]] on the [[Case Western Reserve University]] campus, but not enough to qualify for enrollment at Cleveland State. Bol never played a game for Cleveland State. (Five years later, Cleveland State was placed on two years' probation for providing improper financial assistance to Bol and two other African players.)<ref>{{cite news |last = Associated Press |title = Penalties Upheld for Cleveland State |newspaper = The New York Times |pages = |date = Apr 22, 1988 |url = https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=940DE6D9173AF931A15757C0A96E948260 }}</ref><ref name="auto2">{{cite web|url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/fl-xpm-1985-02-20-8501060790-story.html|title=THE KING DINKA DUNKER: 7-6 HERDSMAN TO NBA?|first=Mitch Albom|last=Columnist|website=Sun-Sentinel.com}}</ref>

===1983 NBA draft voided===

Again, with Feeley's influence, Bol declared his intention to play professionally with the NBA. Subsequently, Bol was drafted by the [[Los Angeles Clippers]] in the fifth round of the [[1983 NBA draft]] (97th overall) after he had declared himself.

Clippers Coach [[Jim Lynam]] received a call about Bol from Coach Feeley, who he knew from coaching circles. "So, I said, 'Have you told anyone else about this?' " Lynam recalled. "Feeley said the only one in the NBA he had called was Frank Layden at Utah. He said Frank said he couldn't take another big guy like this. He already had Mark Eaton. I was the second guy Feeley had called. I told him he didn't have to call anyone else."<ref name="auto3">{{cite web|url=https://www.si.com/vault/1990/12/17/123285/a-tall-story-manute-bol-the-sixers-7-ft7-in-center-views-life-from-a-unique-perspective|title=A TALL STORY|first=Leigh|last=Montville|website=Vault}}</ref>

After the June, 1983 draft, Lynam traveled to Cleveland and watched Manute play in pickup games. In speaking with Bol, through a fellow Sudanese player, Lynam learned that Manute had become hesitant about playing professionally because he did not know the language well enough to understand what his coaches were telling him to do.<ref name="auto3"/>

Lynam noted that, "One of the things everyone was looking at was his passport. His passport said he was 19 years old. His passport also said he was five feet two."

When Lynam asked Bol about the discrepancy with his real height and his passport height, he said that Bol explained that he had been sitting down when measured by Sudan officials.<ref name="auto3"/>

However, language and passport concerns were set aside when the NBA ruled that Bol had not been eligible for the draft and declared the pick invalid. Bol had not declared 45 days before the draft, as required.<ref>{{cite web |last = |first = |authorlink = |title = Manute Bol |work = |publisher = The Draft Review |url = http://www.thedraftreview.com/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=2159 |accessdate = 2012-12-10 }}</ref><ref name="auto1"/><ref name="auto"/>

==College career==
With the NCAA questioning his eligibility for [[NCAA Division I]] basketball, Bol enrolled at the [[University of Bridgeport]], an [[NCAA Division II]] school with an English program for foreign students. There, he played for the Purple Knights in the 1984–1985 season. His coach was [[Bruce Webster]], a friend of Don Feeley. Bol averaged 22.5 points, 13.5 rebounds, and 7.1 blocks per game for Bridgeport. The team, which previously drew 500–600 spectators, routinely sold out the 1,800-seat gym.<ref name="USAToday"/>

With Bol, Bridgeport qualified for the [[1985 NCAA Division II Men's Basketball Tournament]].<ref name="auto2"/>

==Professional basketball career==

Bol turned professional after Bridgeport's season ended, signed with the [[Rhode Island Gulls]] of the spring [[United States Basketball League]] in May 1985, playing under Coach [[Kevin Stacom]]. A teammate, with the Gulls, was [[Muggsy Bogues]] who later would notably team with Bol in Washington.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/05/17/sports/sports-people-bol-may-turn-pro.html|title=SPORTS PEOPLE; Bol May Turn Pro|date=17 May 1985|publisher=|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://articles.latimes.com/1985-07-07/sports/sp-9482_1_gulls|title=Unusual Gulls Are Favorite in This Town|first=Associated|last=Press|date=7 July 1985|publisher=|via=LA Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.si.com/vault/1985/06/24/628058/a-taste-of-high-society|title=A Taste Of High Society|first=Bruce|last=Newman|website=Vault}}</ref>

{{Unreferenced section|date=June 2016}}

Going into the [[1985 NBA draft]], scouts felt that Bol needed another year or two of college, but Bol opted for the draft because he felt that it was the only way to earn enough money to get his sister out of Sudan, which was in a state of political unrest at the time.<ref name="USAToday"/> In 1985, Bol was drafted as the seventh pick in the second round by the Washington Bullets (31st overall). He played in the NBA for ten seasons, from 1985 to 1995, spending parts of four seasons with the Bullets, parts of three with the [[Golden State Warriors]], parts of four with the [[Philadelphia 76ers]], and part of one season with the [[Miami Heat]].

===Washington Bullets I (1985-1988) ===
{{Unreferenced section|date=June 2016}}

On June 18, 1985, Manute Bol was drafted as the seventh pick in the second round by the Washington Bullets (31st overall).<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

Bol's first tenure with the Bullets lasted three seasons, from 1985 to 1988. In his rookie season ([[1985–86 NBA season|1985–1986]]), he appeared in 80 games and recorded a career-high 5.0 blocks per game. His total of 397 blocks set the NBA [[rookie]] record, and remains the second-highest single-season total in league history behind [[Mark Eaton (basketball)|Mark Eaton]]'s 456 in 1984–85.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_1986_leaders.html|title=1985-86 NBA Leaders|website=Basketball-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/blk_season.html|title=NBA & ABA Single Season Leaders and Records for Blocks|website=Basketball-Reference.com}}</ref>

During his NBA career, Bol was listed at {{height|ft=7|in=7}} tall.<ref name="Brown">{{cite book|last= Brown|first= Donald H.|title=A Basketball Handbook|year= 2007|publisher=AuthorHouse| isbn= 978-1-4259-6190-9| page=20|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YJmsqtj-rh4C&pg=PA20| location=Bloomington, Indiana}}</ref> He was measured by the [[Guinness Book of World Records]] at 7 ft 6 3/4 in tall.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kansascity.com/sports/spt-columns-blogs/sam-mellinger/article5352999.html|title=Bol Bol, 14 years old and 6 feet 10, reaches for his father’s heights|author=|date=|website=kansascity|accessdate=7 February 2019}}</ref> Complementing his great [[human height|height]], Bol possessed exceptionally long limbs (inseam {{convert|49|in|cm}}) and large hands and feet ([[Shoe size|size]] 16 {{small|1/2}}). His [[arm span]], at {{convert|8|ft|6|in|m}}, is (as of 2013) the longest in NBA history, and his upward reach was {{convert|10|ft|5|in|m}}.<ref name="WaPo obit"/><ref>{{cite web |title = Former NBA player Manute Bol to speak at Union |publisher = Union College |date = Nov 3, 2008 |url = http://www.union.edu/N/DS/s.php?s=8105 |accessdate = 2012-12-08 }}</ref> He was extremely slender, limiting his offensive capability. When he arrived in the United States, he weighed {{convert|180|lb|kg}}<ref>{{cite news |last = Epting |first = Chris |title = The Manute We Knew: Curious, Shy, One of the Family . . . and a Lion Slayer |newspaper = AOL News |date = Jun 24, 2010 |url = http://www.aolnews.com/2010/06/24/the-manute-we-knew-curious-shy-one-of-the-family/ |archive-url = https://archive.is/20130117040047/http://www.aolnews.com/2010/06/24/the-manute-we-knew-curious-shy-one-of-the-family/ |dead-url = yes |archive-date = January 17, 2013 }}</ref> and had gained just under {{convert|20|lb|kg}} by the time he entered the NBA. The Washington Bullets sent Bol to strength training with [[University of Maryland]] coach Frank Costello, where he could initially lift only {{convert|44|lb|kg}} on 10-repetition [[bench press]] and {{convert|55|lb|kg}} on 10-repetition [[squat (exercise)|squat]]<ref>{{cite journal |last = McCallum |first = Jack |title = Welcome To 'Air Bol': Stronger and heavier, the Bullets' 7'7" Manute Bol could be a force |journal = Sports Illustrated |volume = |issue = |pages = |date = Oct 21, 1985 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1120035/ }}</ref> (his [[body mass index]] was 15.3 and he initially had a 31" (80 cm) waist).<ref>{{cite news |last = McManis |first = Sam |title = At 7 Foot 6, Manute Bol of Sudan Is Surely Rangy Enough for America's City Game and He Has Talent, but at 190 Pounds He May Not Be Strong Enough for Big Time: Basketball's Tallest Story |newspaper = Los Angeles Times |pages = |date = Feb 11, 1985 |url = http://articles.latimes.com/1985-02-11/sports/sp-4394_1_manute-bol }}</ref>
In 1987, the Bullets drafted the {{height|ft=5|in=3}} [[point guard]] [[Muggsy Bogues]], pairing the tallest and shortest players in the league on the court for one season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/07/13/NBA-Bullets-Welcome-Manute-Bol-7-6/6670490075200/|title=NBA Bullets Welcome Manute Bol, 7-6|website=UPI}}</ref><ref name="basketball-reference.com">{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/b/bolma01.html|title=Manute Bol Stats|website=Basketball-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.si.com/nba/photos/2014/10/08/nbas-tallest-and-shortest-together|title=The NBA's Tallest and Shortest Together|website=SI.com}}</ref>

===Golden State Warriors I (1988-1990)===

On June 8, 1988, Bol was traded by the Bullets to the Golden State Warriors for [[Dave Feitl]] and a 1989 2nd round draft pick ([[Doug Roth]] was later selected).<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

Bol's first tenure with the Golden State Warriors lasted for two seasons, from 1988 to 1990. In his first season with Golden State, he first attempted three-point shots with regularity. In that season, he shot a career-high 91 three-pointers and made 20 of them. During this time, he may have helped to popularize the expression "[[wikt:my bad|my bad]]", although a 2005 suggestion that he coined the phrase has been discounted.<ref name="Pullum">{{cite web|url=http://itre.cis.upenn.edu/~myl/languagelog/archives/002693.html|title=Language Log: Pick-up basketballism reaches Ivy League faculty vocabulary|last=Pullum|first=Geoffrey K. |authorlink=Geoff Pullum |date=7 December 2005|accessdate=2010-06-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.visualthesaurus.com/cm/wordroutes/2327/|title=The Manute Bol Theory of "My Bad"|last=Zimmer|first=Ben |authorlink=Ben Zimmer |date=22 June 2010|work=Word Routes|publisher=Thinkmap Visual Thesaurus|accessdate=2010-06-23}}</ref>

===Philadelphia 76ers I (1990-1993)===
On August 1, 1990, Bol was traded by Golden State to the Philadelphia 76ers for a 1991 1st round draft pick ([[Chris Gatling]] was later selected).<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

Bol's first tenure with the Philadelphia 76ers lasted for three seasons, from 1990 to 1993. Although he played in a career-high 82 games in his first season as a 76er, his production began to decline afterward (in both games played and per-game statistics). After playing in all 82 games in [[1990–91 NBA season|1990–1991]], he played in 71 games the [[1991–92 NBA season|next season]], and in 58 (a career low at the time) games the [[1992–93 NBA season|following season]]. During his last season in Philadelphia, he had a memorable night playing against former teammate [[Charles Barkley]] and the Phoenix Suns, hitting 6 of 12 three-pointers, all in the second half in a losing effort.<ref>{{cite web |title = Philadelphia 76ers at Phoenix Suns Box Score, March 3, 1993 |work = Basketball Reference.com |publisher = Sports Reference |url = https://www.basketball-reference.com/boxscores/PHO19930303.html |accessdate = 2012-12-10 |deadurl = yes |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20071216132101/http://www.basketball-reference.com/boxscores/PHO19930303.html |archivedate = December 16, 2007 |df = }}</ref> Fans were known to yell out "shoot" as soon as Bol received the ball far from the basket.<ref>Kerry Eggers, "Around the League", The Sunday Oregonian, March 7, 1993</ref>

===Miami Heat (1993)===
Released by Philadelphia, Bol played in eight games in the [[1993–94 NBA season|1993–1994 season]] with the [[Miami Heat]], the only team that did not use him as a starter. He scored only one two-point field goal with the team and blocked six shots in 61 total minutes.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/b/bolma01.html|title=Manute Bol Stats {{!}} Basketball-Reference.com|website=Basketball-Reference.com|language=en|access-date=2018-02-09}}</ref>

===Washington Bullets II (1993)===
Released by Miami, Bol's second stint with the Bullets lasted only two games in 1993–1994. After this, he helped develop fellow 7 ft 7 teammate [[Gheorghe Mureșan]].<ref name=":0" />

===Philadelphia 76ers II (1994)===
After his release by Miami, Bol's second stint with the 76ers lasted for four games, near the end of the 1993–1994 season, helping to mentor {{height|ft=7|in=6}} teammate [[Shawn Bradley]]. In only 49 minutes, he played more aggressively than he did earlier in the season with Miami and Washington. He scored six points, grabbed six rebounds and blocked nine shots.<ref name=":0" />

===Golden State Warriors II (1994)===
In the [[1994–95 NBA season]], Bol returned to the Warriors. He made the season-opening roster and played in what would be his final five NBA games. On a memorable night in the middle of November, Bol finally made his home debut, coming off of the bench to play 29 minutes against the Minnesota Timberwolves. Bol attempted three three-pointers in the fourth quarter, scoring all of them.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/b/bolma01/gamelog/1995/|title=Manute Bol 1994-95 Game Log {{!}} Basketball-Reference.com|website=Basketball-Reference.com|language=en|access-date=2018-02-09}}</ref> Seven nights later in Charlotte, in a game that was nationally televised by [[Turner Network Television|TNT]], he was in the starting lineup again. By this time, two weeks into the season, his career seemed rejuvenated under Warrior head coach [[Don Nelson]]; he was again a defensive force, making threes and contributing as a starter to create matchup problems. After playing only ten minutes against the Hornets on November 22, 1994, he suffered a season-ending knee injury. Before he left the game, he recorded one block and two points and attempted a three-pointer in ten minutes of play.<ref name=":1" />

Bol was waived by Golden State on February 15, 1995.<ref name=":0" />

Overall in his NBA career, Bol averaged 2.6 points, 4.2 rebounds, 0.3 assists, and 3.3 blocks per game, while playing an average of 18.7 minutes. Bol finished his career with totals of 1,599 points, 2,647 rebounds, and 2,086 blocks. He appeared in 624 games over 10 seasons.<ref>{{cite web |publisher = basketball-reference.com |title = Manute Bol |url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/b/bolma01.html |accessdate = 2008-05-29 }}</ref>

===Post-NBA basketball career (1995-1998)===
Bol played 22 games for the [[Florida Beach Dogs]] of the [[Continental Basketball Association]] during the 1995–1996 season under Coach [[Eric Musselman]]. The Beach Dogs' games against the [[Sioux Falls Skyforce]] in that season were broadcast by [[ESPN]], as the Skyforce also featured a former NBA player, [[Darryl Dawkins]].<ref name="SI 01"/>

In 1996, the [[Portland Wave|Portland Mountain Cats]] of the [[United States Basketball League]] announced that Bol would be playing with the team, but he never appeared in uniform. The coach of the Mountain Cats was Kevin Mackey.<ref name="SI 01"/><ref>http://maineprosports.com/history-of-the-portland-mountain-cats/</ref>

Bol played professionally in [[Italy]] in 1997 and in [[Qatar]] in 1998 before [[rheumatism]] forced him to retire permanently.<ref name="SI 01"/>

==Shot blocking==
With his great height and very long limbs, Bol was one of the league's most imposing defensive presences. Along with setting the rookie shot-blocking record in 1985–86, over the course of his career, Bol tied for the NBA record for the most blocked shots in one half (11) and in one quarter (eight, twice).<ref>{{cite web |title = Regular Season Records: Blocked Shots |work = NBA Encyclopedia |publisher = National Basketball Association |url = http://www.nba.com/history/records/regular_blockedshots.html |accessdate = 2012-12-10 }}</ref> On {{Dts|1992|January|31}}, in a game against the [[Orlando Magic]], he blocked four consecutive shots within a single possession.<ref name="FSN">{{cite episode |title = Manute Bol: Beyond the Glory |episodelink = |url = |series = |serieslink = |credits = |network = FOX Sports Net |station = |city = |airdate = Apr 17, 2005 |began = |ended = |season = |seriesno = |number = |minutes = |transcript = |transcripturl= }}</ref> Throughout his career, he blocked a shot an average of every 5.6 minutes of playing time.<ref name="SI 01">{{cite journal |last = Anderson |first = Kelli |title = Manute Bol: Once the NBA's premier shot blocker, the Sudanese Sultan of Swat has tried to bring peace to his homeland |journal = Sports Illustrated |volume = |issue = |pages = |date = Jul 2, 2001 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1022915/ }}</ref>

However, Bol's other basketball skills were very limited, and his rail-thin physique made it difficult for him to establish position against the league's bulkier centers and power forwards. The sight of the tall, gangly Bol spotting up for a three-pointer during blow-outs became a fan favorite. Off the court, he established a reputation as a practical joker; Charles Barkley, a frequent victim of his pranks, attested to Bol's sense of humor.<ref>{{cite web | last = Narducci | first = Marc | title = Tough Time for a Tall Guy His sense of humor could be a help to Manute Bol as he seeks to recover his health after a serious car crash. | publisher = Philly.com | date = Jul 8, 2005 | url = http://articles.philly.com/2004-07-18/sports/25371302_1_manute-bol-neville-h-robinson-sixers }}</ref> Bol also developed a close friendship with Warriors teammate [[Chris Mullin (basketball)|Chris Mullin]] and named one of his sons after him.

==Career accomplishments==
Bol was one of the two tallest players in the history of the [[National Basketball Association]]; the other is [[Gheorghe Mureșan]].<ref name="Brown"/> 

As of 2010, Bol remains:
* First in career blocks per 48 minutes (8.6), almost 50% beyond second-place [[Mark Eaton (basketball)|Mark Eaton]] (5.8).<ref>{{cite web |title = Career Leaders for Blocks Per 48 Minute |work = Basketball Reference.com |publisher = Sports Reference |url = https://www.basketball-reference.com/play-index/psl_finder.cgi?request=1&sum=1&type=per_minute&per_minute_base=48&is_playoffs=N&year_min=1947&year_max=2010&season_start=1&season_end=-1&age_min=0&age_max=99&height_min=0&height_max=99&lg_id=&franch_id=&is_active=&is_hof=&pos=&qual=&c1stat=mp&c1comp=gt&c1val=1000&c2stat=&c2comp=gt&c2val=&c3stat=&c3comp=gt&c3val=&c4stat=&c4comp=gt&c4val=&order_by=blk_per_mp |accessdate = 2012-12-14 }}</ref>
* Second in career blocks-per-game average (3.34).<ref>{{cite web |title = Career Leaders and Records for Blocks Per Game |work = Basketball Reference.com |publisher = Sports Reference |url = https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/BPG_career.html |accessdate = 2012-12-14 }}</ref>
* Fifteenth in total blocked shots (2,086).<ref name="blk_career">{{cite web |title = Career Leaders and Records for Blocks |work = Basketball Reference.com |publisher = Sports Reference |url = https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/BLK_career.html |accessdate = 2012-12-14 }}</ref>
* The only player in NBA history to have more blocked shots than points scored.<ref name="blk_career"/>

==Activism==
Bol was very active in charitable causes throughout his career. In fact, he said he spent much of the money he made during a 10-year NBA career supporting various causes related to the war-ravaged nation of his birth, Sudan.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Zumoff |first=Marc |title=Catching up with Manute Bol |journal=Drive |volume= |issue= |pages= |publisher=NBA Media Ventures |url=http://www.nba.com/sixers/features/drive_manute_bol_070807.html |deadurl=yes |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215162830/http://www.nba.com/sixers/features/drive_manute_bol_070807.html |archivedate=2007-12-15 |df= }}</ref> 

Bol frequently visited Sudanese refugee camps, where he was treated like royalty. In 2001, Bol was offered a post as minister of sport by the Sudanese government. Bol, who was a Christian,<ref>{{cite news |last = Shields |first = Jon A. |title = Manute Bol's radical Christianity |newspaper = The Wall Street Journal |pages = |date = Jun 25, 2010 |url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748704853404575323043046894012 }}</ref> refused because one of the conditions was converting to [[Islam]].<ref name="focusdep.com">{{cite web|last=Luo |first=Michael |title=NBA Star Now Refugee |agency=Associated Press |url=http://www.focusdep.com/articles/Society/NBA_Star_Now_Refugee |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070223041640/http://www.focusdep.com/articles/Society/NBA_Star_Now_Refugee |dead-url=yes |archive-date=2007-02-23 |accessdate= }}</ref> 

Later, Bol was hindered from leaving the country by the Sudanese government, who accused him of supporting the Dinka-led Christian rebels, the [[Sudan People's Liberation Army]]. The Sudanese government refused to grant him an exit visa unless he came back with more money. Assistance by supporters in the United States, including [[Connecticut]] Senator [[Joseph Lieberman]], raised money to provide Bol with plane tickets to Cairo, Egypt. After 6 months of negotiations with U.S. consulate officials regarding refugee status, Bol and his family were finally able to leave Egypt and return to the United States.<ref name="focusdep.com"/>

Bol established the [[Ring True Foundation]] to continue fund-raising for [[Sudanese refugees]]. He gave most of his earnings (an estimated $3.5 million) to their cause. In 2002, [[Fox TV]] agreed to broadcast the telephone number of his Ring True Foundation in exchange for Bol's agreement to appear on their ''[[Celebrity Boxing]]'' show. After the referee goaded, "If you guys don't box, you won't get paid", he scored a third-round victory over former [[American football|football]] player [[William Perry (American football)|William "The Refrigerator" Perry]].

In the fall of 2002, Bol signed a one-day contract with the [[Indianapolis Ice]] of the [[Central Hockey League]]. Though he could not skate, the publicity generated by his single-game appearance helped raise money to assist children in Sudan.<ref>{{cite book|first=Jon C.|last=Scott|title=Hockey Night in Dixie: Minor Pro Hockey in the American South|year=2006|publisher=Heritage House Publishing Company Ltd.|page=184|isbn = 1-894974-21-2 }}</ref> Bol once suited up as a horse jockey for similar reasons.

Bol was involved in the April 2006 [[Sudan Freedom Walk]], a three-week march from the [[United Nations]] building in New York City to the [[United States Capitol]] in Washington, DC. The event was organized by [[Simon Deng]], a former Sudanese swimming champion (currently a lifeguard at [[Coney Island]]), who was a longtime friend of Bol's. Deng, who was a [[Slavery|slave]] for three years from the age of nine, is from another tribe in Southern Sudan. His Sudan Freedom Walk is especially aimed at finding a solution to the [[genocide]] in [[Darfur]] (western Sudan), but it also seeks to raise awareness of the modern-day slavery and human-rights abuses throughout Sudan. Bol spoke in New York City at the start of the walk, and in [[Philadelphia]] at a rally organized by former hunger striker [[Nathan Kleinman]].

Bol was also an advocate for reconciliation efforts, and worked to improve education in South Sudan. A Nicholas Kristoff article<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/24/opinion/24kristof.html?_r=3&ref=nicholasdkristof |newspaper=The New York Times |first=Nicholas D. |last=Kristof |title=Most Valuable Helper |date=Jun 23, 2010}}</ref> in ''The New York Times'' highlighted this belief and Bol's work for reconciliation and education with an organization called [[Sudan Sunrise]]. Bol first began working with Sudan Sunrise to raise awareness on issues of reconciliation in 2005. This included speaking at the United States Capitol in Washington, DC, and subsequently partnering with Sudan Sunrise to build schools across South Sudan that, in the spirit of reconciliation, would enroll students regardless of tribe or religion.<ref>{{cite web |title = Manute Bol School |work = Current Projects in South Sudan |publisher = Sudan Sunrise |url = http://www.sudansunrise.org/project/manute-bol-school |accessdate = 2012-12-14 }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Bol had six children with his first wife, Along, and four with his second wife, Ajok.<ref>{{cite news |last = McGeehan |first = Patrick |title = Manute Bol, N.B.A. Player and Activist, Dies at 47 |newspaper = The New York Times |pages = |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/20/sports/basketball/20bol.html?scp=2 }}</ref>

Bol's son, Madut (born December 19, 1989), played college basketball at [[Southern Jaguars basketball|Southern University]] and graduated from college in 2013.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/basketball/nba/2010-06-29-manute-bol-funeral_N.htm|title=Manute Bol remembered as 'also a giant off the court' at funeral|date=June 29, 2010|work=USA Today|accessdate=March 23, 2014}}</ref> 

Another son, [[Bol Bol]] (born November 16, 1999), played for the [[Oregon Ducks men's basketball|Oregon Ducks]] in 2018-2019. Bol Bol declared for the [[2019 NBA draft]] and is projected to be a first-round pick.<ref>{{cite web |title=NBA Draft 2019 Best Remaining Players - ESPN Draftcast |url=http://www.espn.com/nba/draft/bestavailable |website=ESPN.com |accessdate=4 February 2019 |language=en}}</ref>

During his time in Egypt, Bol ran a basketball school in [[Cairo]]. One of his pupils was a fellow Sudanese refugee, [[Minnesota Timberwolves]] player [[Luol Deng]], the son of a former Sudanese cabinet minister. Deng later moved to the United States to further his basketball career, continuing a close relationship with Bol.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/page/blackhistoryNBA1|title=Wallace: Luol Deng's path of righteousness|date=26 February 2015|website=ESPN.com}}</ref>

Despite initially knowing little English and an absence of awareness regarding Western culture, Bol adjusted and was widely regarded as a well-rounded personality who was inquisitive and well-read. He developed a strong friendship with Charles Barkley, who remarked, "If everyone in the world was a Manute Bol, it's a world I'd want to live in. He's smart. He reads ''The New York Times''. He knows what's going on in a lot of subjects. He's not one of these just-basketball guys".<ref name="SI 90">{{cite journal |last = Montville |first = Leigh |title = A Tall Story: Manute Bol, the Sixers' 7'7" center, views life from a unique perspective |journal = Sports Illustrated |volume = |issue = |pages = |date = Dec 17, 1990 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1136052/ }}</ref>

Bol spoke [[Dinka language|Dinka]] and [[Arabic language|Arabic]] before mastering English.<ref>{{cite journal |last = Lidz |first = Franz |title = Come See The Dinka Dunker Do: Manute Bol, an import from Sudan, is giving a 7'6" lift to Bridgeport |journal = Sports Illustrated |volume = |issue = |pages = |date = Dec 10, 1984 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1122922/ }}</ref>

After a political dispute in Sudan, Bol was admitted to the United States as a religious refugee in 2002 and settled in [[West Hartford, Connecticut]].<ref name="WaPo obit"/>

In July 2004, Bol was seriously injured in a car accident in [[Colchester, Connecticut|Colchester]] when he was ejected from a taxi that hit a guardrail and overturned, resulting in a broken neck.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Fox|first1=Tracy Gordon|last2=Farrell|first2=Jim|title=Bol critically injured in car accident|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1914&dat=20040702&id=GxAqAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nmQFAAAAIBAJ&pg=1174,283134|accessdate=8 July 2014|work=The Hartford Courant|date=2 July 2014}}</ref> The driver was under the influence, with a suspended license.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://compuserve.nba.com/sixers/features/manute_bol_060822.html|title=Where Are They Now: Manute Bol|publisher=|accessdate=27 August 2017|deadurl=yes|archiveurl=https://archive.is/20120709140413/http://compuserve.nba.com/sixers/features/manute_bol_060822.html|archivedate=9 July 2012|df=}}</ref> Because his fortunes were mostly donated to Sudan, he was financially ruined because he had no health insurance.<ref name="FSN"/> When he recovered from his injuries, he moved to [[Olathe, Kansas]].<ref name="WaPo obit"/>

==Death==
On June 19, 2010, Bol died from [[acute kidney failure]] and complications from [[Stevens–Johnson syndrome]] at the [[University of Virginia Health System|University of Virginia Medical Center]] in [[Charlottesville, Virginia]].<ref name="WaPo obit">{{cite news|last=Schudel|first=Matt |title=Manute Bol, former Washington Bullet and one of NBA's tallest players, dies at 47|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/19/AR2010061902214.html|accessdate=19 June 2010|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=19 June 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.pitch.com/plog/2010/06/manute_bol_retired_basketball_player_has_died.php |title=Manute Bol, retired basketball player, has died |last=Kendall |first=Justin |date=June 19, 2010 |accessdate=2010-06-19 |publisher=The Pitch |deadurl=yes |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100622032557/http://blogs.pitch.com/plog/2010/06/manute_bol_retired_basketball_player_has_died.php |archivedate=June 22, 2010 |df= }}</ref> 

After his death, tributes to Bol's basketball career and charitable works came from around the United States and the world.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://voices.washingtonpost.com/local-opinions/2010/06/manute_bols_other_legacy.html | work=The Washington Post |title=Manute Bol's other legacy}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/gallery/2010/06/19/GA2010061902220.html |work=The Washington Post|title=Manute Bol, former Washington Bullet: 1962-2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.boston.com/sports/basketball/articles/2010/06/22/manute_bol_had_height_of_course_but_even_more_depth |work=The Boston Globe |title=Height, and depth |first=Bob |last=Ryan |date=June 22, 2010}}</ref> His former teams, and the NBA, issued statements in recognition of his impact on the sport of basketball and on his native Sudan.<ref>{{cite web |last = Leonsis |first = Ted |title = Ted Leonsis' Statement on Passing of Manute Bol |work = Washington Wizards news |publisher = NBA Media Ventures |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = http://www.nba.com/wizards/news/bol_100619.html |accessdate = 2012-12-14 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title = Former Warrior Manute Bol Passes Away |work = Golden State Warriors news |publisher = NBA Media Ventures |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = http://www.nba.com/warriors/news/bol_passes_away_061810.html |accessdate = 2012-12-14 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last = Stefanski |first = Ed |title = Philadelphia 76ers statement on the passing of Manute Bol |work = Philadelphia 76ers news |publisher = NBA Media Ventures |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = http://www.nba.com/sixers/news/bol_100619.html |accessdate = 2012-12-14 }}</ref> Kansas senator [[Sam Brownback]] paid tribute to Bol on the floor of the United States Senate after his death.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/video/2010/06/22/VI2010062202905.html |newspaper=The Washington Post |title=Video: A Senate salute to Manute |date=2010-06-22}}</ref>

Bol is buried in [[South Sudan]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kmbc.com/news/24214449/detail.html|title=Memorial To Honor Manute Bol|publisher=|accessdate=27 August 2017|deadurl=yes|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307131045/http://www.kmbc.com/news/24214449/detail.html|archivedate=7 March 2012|df=}}</ref>

===Funeral service and tributes===
[[File:Manute Bol's funeral at National Cathedral 2010-06-29 1.jpg|thumb|Bol's memorial service at the National Cathedral]]

The memorial service for Manute Bol was held on Tuesday, June 29, 2010, at 10:00 am at the National Cathedral in Washington, DC. Bol's body lay in an eight-foot-long, specially built casket.<ref name="google.com">[https://www.google.com/hostednews/canadianpress/article/ALeqM5j4CZIgXsXmROD8dYFKNNhS3BpA2w] {{dead link|date=September 2016}}</ref>

Bol was given tributes by United States Senator [[Sam Brownback]] from Kansas, former National Security Advisor [[Robert McFarlane]], Sudan's Ambassador to the United States, Dr. Akec Khoc Acieu, Bol's uncle Bol Bol Chol, and vice president of the [[National Basketball Players Association]] [[Rory Sparrow]].<ref name="google.com" />

Sparrow remembered Bol as "a giant off the court", who should be remembered for humanitarian work and his basketball career.<ref name="google.com" /> Senator Brownback recalled, "He literally gave his life for his people. He went over [to Sudan], he was sick. He stayed longer than he should have. He probably contracted this ailment that took his life while in Sudan, and he didn't have to do that. He was an NBA basketball player. He could have stayed here and had an easy life. I've never seen anybody use his celebrity status more nor give his life more completely to a group of people than Manute Bol did. It makes me look at efforts that I do as not enough."

Dr. Akec K.A. Khoc, Ambassador of Sudan to the U.S., said, "Manute had a very great heart for his country and people. He did everything to support anybody in need of shoes, blankets, health service, food, and people who were struggling. He went to see them and to encourage them to continue their struggle for their rights, for their freedoms. Manute embodied everything we can think of in Sudan. Reconciling warring groups between the north and south, in Darfur he was working for reconciliation between Darfur and the south and between Darfur and the rest of Sudan. So, Manute was a voice for hope."

[[Sudan Sunrise]] founder, Tom Prichard, says Bol's work to reconcile former enemies lives on. "Manute's legacy and vision of education and reconciliation, his determination to grow [[grassroots]] reconciliation—whether that reconciliation is expressed in a country that divides or holds together, wherever the boundary lines are drawn. Manute stood for grassroots reconciliation."<ref name="www1.voanews.com">{{cite news |title=Dignitaries, Friends Say Farewell to NBA's Manute Bol |publisher=VOA News |date=Jun 28, 2010 |url=http://www1.voanews.com/english/news/africa/Dignitaries-Friends-say-Farewell-to-NBA-Manute-Bol-97432534.html |accessdate=2012-12-14}}</ref> Prichard went on to say "There's no question Manute gave his life for his country."<ref name="kansascity.com">http://www.kansascity.com/2010/06/22/2036636/nba-legend-spent-his-life-helping.html</ref><ref name="kansascity.com" />

Manute Bol's family [[patriarch]], Bol Bol Chol, said, "This man is not an ordinary man. I believe this man is a messenger like other messengers who were sent into this world—to do something in this world. He has accomplished most of his mission, and so God took him and left the rest of the work to be done by others."<ref name="www1.voanews.com" />

* Bol was inducted into the University of Bridgeport Athletics Hall of Fame, Class of 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bridgeport.edu/news/2010-09-21/university-bridgeport-set-induct-four-new-members-ub-athletic-hall-fame-november-6|title=University of Bridgeport set to induct four new members into the UB Athletic Hall of Fame on November 6, 2010 - University of Bridgeport|website=bridgeport.edu}}</ref>

* On January 27 2015, the Golden State Warriors honored Bol with a Manute Bol bobble head giveaway. The team sponsored a giveaway of 10,000 of the tallest bobble heads in franchise history, at 10 inches.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://abc7news.com/sports/warriors-honor-manute-bol-with-bobblehead/493801/|title=Warriors honor Manute Bol with bobblehead|date=28 January 2015|website=ABC7 San Francisco}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nba.com/warriors/news/manute-bol-bobblehead-night-20150127|title=Warriors to Host Manute Bol Bobblehead Night on Tuesday, January 27 Against the Chicago Bulls|website=Golden State Warriors}}</ref>

* The "Manute Bol Court" was built and constructed in South Sudan by the Loul Deng Foundation in 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://beyondsport.org/articles/the-loul-deng-foundation-opens-the-manute-bol-court-in-south-sudan/|title=Beyond Sport|website=beyondsport.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sportingnews.com/us/nba/news/luol-deng-manute-bol-court-south-sudan-picture-instagram/xyqo3igvj66m1x24pfclvaw23|title=Luol Deng: South Sudan court among 'most memorable' accomplishments|date=10 August 2015|website=Sporting News}}</ref>

* The Manute Bol Peace Builders Basketball Tournament is held annually throughout Sudan.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.voanews.com/a/south-sudan-organizes-manute-bol-basketball-tournament/2828742.html|title=Basketball Tournament Honors Manute Bol|website=VOA}}</ref>

* In 2016, Bol was inducted into the Fairfield County Sports Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sudansunrise.org/fairfield-county-hall-fame-honors-manute-bol/|title=Fairfield County Hall of Fame Honors Manute Bol|date=19 October 2016|publisher=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.greenwichtime.com/sports/article/Sports-Night-dinner-honors-Hall-of-Fame-inductees-9979373.php|title=Sports Night dinner honors Hall of Fame inductees|first=David|last=Fierro|date=18 October 2016|website=GreenwichTime}}</ref>
